title: Jharkhand Student Protests Enter Day 14 as Hunger Strikes Continue and National Leaders Step In
excerpt: An 11-member student delegation has begun talks with the Hemant Soren government, but the agitation over JPSC and JSSC exam irregularities shows no signs of ending.
body:
• The Jharkhand student protests over alleged irregularities in JPSC and JSSC recruitment exams have entered their 14th day, with hunger strikes continuing at Ranchi's Jaipal Singh Munda Stadium and an 11-member student delegation formed for talks with the state government.
  • The monsoon session of the Jharkhand Assembly began on August 6 amid opposition protests and police detaining 19 demonstrators, while Congress leaders Rahul Gandhi and Mallikarjun Kharge publicly backed the students' demands.
  • Students are demanding cancellation of the 14th JPSC Preliminary Examination, a CBI probe into alleged paper leaks and recruitment irregularities, and a transparent overhaul of the state's examination system.

The student-led protests that erupted in Jharkhand on July 29 over alleged irregularities in state recruitment examinations have escalated into one of the largest youth movements the state has seen, entering their 14th day on Thursday with hunger strikes, political interventions, and the start of formal talks between an 11-member student delegation and the Hemant Soren-led government.

Thousands of job aspirants and students remain camped at Ranchi's Jaipal Singh Munda Stadium, demanding the cancellation of the 14th Jharkhand Public Service Commission (JPSC) Preliminary Examination, a CBI investigation into alleged paper leaks, and a transparent overhaul of the state's recruitment machinery.

What Sparked the Protests

The agitation centers on allegations of irregularities and question paper leaks in examinations conducted by the JPSC and the Jharkhand Staff Selection Commission (JSSC). A viral answer sheet circulating on social media in late July triggered the initial sit-in, which quickly snowballed as students arrived from across the state. Protesters say the recruitment process has been compromised by corruption, and have demanded that the government hold accountable those responsible.

The demands are specific: cancel the 14th JPSC Preliminary Examination, order a CBI or judicial inquiry into the alleged irregularities, ensure transparency in future examinations, and take action against officials involved in the recruitment process.

Assembly Session Begins Amid Chaos

The Jharkhand Assembly's monsoon session began on August 6 with opposition parties staging protests inside the legislature over the recruitment controversy. Police detained 19 people during demonstrations near the assembly. Students had earlier announced plans for a Tiranga (tricolor) March and a gherao of the Jharkhand Assembly on August 10, raising the prospect of further escalation.

"We are children, not terrorists."

— Students on hunger strike, addressing Chief Minister Hemant Soren

Political Support Widens

The protests have drawn support from across the political spectrum. Congress President Mallikarjun Kharge and leader Rahul Gandhi both publicly backed the students on August 7, with Gandhi reaching out specifically to Gen Z protesters — the demographic that dominates the movement. BJP MP Nishikant Dubey has demanded a CBI inquiry, while opposition leaders in the Jharkhand Assembly have repeatedly raised the issue.

Shashi Tharoor, the Congress leader, noted that the movement has resonated more broadly with students than some Delhi-centered protests, pointing to the organic, non-partisan character of the Jharkhand agitation.

Government Responds With Talks

The Jharkhand government initiated talks with protesting students on August 6, after the student body formed an 11-member delegation to negotiate. The initial meeting, however, proved inconclusive, with students saying they would continue their agitation until concrete action was taken. The government pledged to consider complaints and seek solutions through dialogue, while security was tightened across Ranchi.

Why NRIs Are Watching

Recruitment exam scandals have become a recurring flashpoint in Indian politics, with movements in Bihar, Uttar Pradesh, and now Jharkhand driven by a generation of young Indians who see government jobs as their primary path to economic stability. For the Indian diaspora — many of whom have family members navigating these examination systems — the Jharkhand protests represent a larger crisis of institutional trust that extends well beyond one state's borders.
